summary: This Stack Overflow page captures the question 'How to run a PowerShell script' asked in 2010 by a user who could not get a .ps1 file to run via powershell.exe from a batch file, with the command returning only the file name. The page collects many answers, with the top-voted one explaining how to run a script from within an administrator PowerShell session after changing the execution policy, and another showing how to call powershell.exe with -File or with a call operator from cmd.exe. Other answers cover execution policy bypass switches, running scripts via Windows Task Scheduler, PowerShell ISE, and right-clicking a .ps1 file to run it with PowerShell.
one_line: Stack Overflow Q&A collecting answers on running PowerShell .ps1 scripts from PowerShell, cmd, batch files, and Task Scheduler, including execution policy handling.
key_facts: The question was asked on January 9, 2010 and had about 1022 votes and 3.0 million views when captured.
The asker had a script named myscript.ps1 and ran it with powershell.exe 'C:\my_path\yada_yada\run_import_script.ps1', which returned only the file name with no error.
The top-voted answer says to launch Windows PowerShell as an Administrator, navigate to the script directory with cd, and execute it with .\run_import_script.ps1.
The top-voted answer gives the cmd.exe form: powershell -noexit "& ""C:\my_path\yada_yada\run_import_script.ps1""", citing Kirk Munro's post on invoking a PowerShell script from cmd.exe.
The answer by Keith Hill states that on PowerShell 2.0, the -File parameter of PowerShell.exe can invoke a script from another environment such as cmd.exe.
Keith Hill advises adding -ExecutionPolicy Bypass if script execution is disabled on the system.
Chingiz Musayev's answer gives the form powershell [-noexit] -executionpolicy bypass -File <Filename> to run a script without modifying the default execution policy.
An answer by AndyM says that on PowerShell 1.0, piping the file works: powershell -command - < c:\mypath\myscript.ps1.
An answer by electronictonic says that right-clicking a .ps1 file in Windows and choosing Run with PowerShell runs the script.
An answer by JovanToroman recommends running set-executionpolicy unrestricted in administrator mode and then running set-ExecutionPolicy default afterward to avoid security risks.
An answer by Eugene describes creating a Windows Task Scheduler task with Program/Script set to Powershell.exe and Arguments set to -File "C:\xxx.ps1".
An answer by rainabba says that on Windows 10 with PowerShell version 5.1, typing ./myscript.ps1 in a PowerShell window runs the script.

An answer by Roukmoute shows the command Microsoft uses for right-click Run with PowerShell, which sets the execution policy to Bypass for the Process scope before running the script with the call operator &.
Marc_s's answer notes that the powershell -noexit form was needed because of quoting, and the asker reported that three double quotes around the path worked.
